question: Under the baked-in step skeleton (Register + N authored work steps + verification/full-suite/close-out), how many authored WORK steps N may a session declare? The 5-step cap measured by Set 111 S4 was taken on specs whose 5 declared steps already absorbed the ceremony, so it cannot be carried over unexamined: historical '5 declared' meant roughly 3-4 real work steps, while '4 + N' declared now contains only N.
decision: N = 3 authored work steps, so 7 declared steps per session (authoring.max_steps_per_session = 7). 3 is the value that holds the Set 111 S4 measured 42-minute median once the ceremony is subtracted. The operator's opening suggestion of N = 4 was put to the operator alongside it and REJECTED at ratification: it is a deliberate loosening rather than a re-count, and sessionSizeException already exists for genuine overruns.

options.option: N = 3 authored work steps (7 declared).
options.consequence: Holds the measured 42-minute median: Set 111 S4 found 1-5 declared steps ran a 42-min median / 110-min p90 / 10% over two hours, and those specs spent about two of their declared steps on ceremony, so 3 real work steps is the middle of the measured band rather than its edge. Costs authors a split, or a declared sessionSizeException, on the fourth work step. Reversible: the cap is one integer in router-config.yaml.

options.option: N = 4 authored work steps (8 declared) - the operator's opening suggestion.
options.consequence: A deliberate loosening past the measured band. Set 111 S4's 6-8 declared band ran an 84-minute median with a 386-minute p90 and 28% of sessions past two hours; while those 8 declared steps were more work-dense than 4+4 would be, nothing in the measurement supports 4 work steps, so it would arrive as an artifact of re-counting rather than as evidence. Also reversible, but it sets the looser number as the baseline everyone anchors on.

options.option: Carry the number 5 over unchanged.
options.consequence: Silently loosens the real budget from 3-4 work steps to 5 while appearing to change nothing, because the same integer now counts four ceremony steps it did not count before. This is the failure the re-baselining exists to prevent.

operator_attestation: Operator ratified N = 3 on 2026-08-12 at the Session 1 registration stop, from an education-mode brief that named N = 4 as their own opening suggestion and the Set 111 S4 measurement as the evidence. Recorded because the source-of-record note marks the question 'Unresolved - the operator skipped the question'.

question: The step-shape check lands against a corpus of 45 specs / 363 planned sessions of which exactly 3 conform - and all 3 are this set's own. Does the check BLOCK the existing non-conforming corpus, report it, or apply only to new sets?
decision: Blocking for sets that have not started; an informational note for every set that has already started, completed, or was cancelled. A set is 'not started' when it has no session-state.json or its status is not-started - the same file the repo already treats as the single source of truth for set progress. The blocking verdict is named 'requires restructuring', never 'refused'. Per the operator, the note on already-started sets is explicitly NOT a warning: those specs were authored under a different approach at a different time, and nothing about them is wrong.

options.option: Requires-restructuring (blocking) for unstarted sets; informational note for started/complete/cancelled sets.
options.consequence: Bites on day one - 113, 118, 121 and 122 are unstarted and non-conforming, so the check has something it genuinely fails, and a brand-new spec with no state file at all is the primary authoring-time path. The restructuring cost lands only where it is cheapest (an unstarted spec is a text edit, and 118's is already scheduled for Session 3). Costs one read of session-state.json inside a previously pure-text checker. Reversible: the gating predicate is one function.

options.option: Advisory everywhere - the check reports the shape but never fails.
options.consequence: Nothing can fail it on day one, which is exactly the shape L-112-1 warns about: a gate that only ever passes is indistinguishable from one that checks nothing. It would also leave the unstarted sets free to be executed under the old assumptions, which is the race this set exists to prevent.

options.option: Blocking everywhere - every spec must conform.
options.consequence: Fails 360 of 363 planned sessions and breaks 'spec_admission --all --check' in CI immediately. Retrofitting 40+ historical specs is a declared non-goal of this set and would be meaningless, since their sessions are closed and rewriting their step text changes nothing that will ever run.

options.option: Silently grandfather everything that predates the check.
options.consequence: Explicitly excluded by the source-of-record note: that is how the check ends up proving nothing. Not put to the operator.

operator_attestation: Operator ratified on 2026-08-12 at the Session 1 registration stop: 'Blocking for unstarted sets, but an information note for the rest -- don't suggest a warning. It was a different time and a different approach. Leave it at that.' The operator separately ruled the verdict be called 'require restructuring' rather than 'refuse'.

question: A4.1 and A4.2 (operator ruling, 2026-08-12) change what a post-suite fix owes: a fix to tests only triggers no re-verification, and a fix to shipped code triggers a targeted remediation-review rather than an open re-verification. That REDUCES verification and is the constitution's hard carve-out, so it cannot be inferred from the source-of-record note by an orchestrator. Is it ratified for encoding in this repo's rules and machinery, and is the superseded 'less than two lines' formulation withdrawn?
decision: Ratified as ruled, keyed on WHAT changed rather than on how large the change is. A4.1: a post-suite fix touching only test surfaces owes no re-verification. A4.2: a post-suite fix touching shipped code owes one delta-scoped `verify_session --phase remediation-review`, not an open re-verification. The earlier 'less than two lines' formulation is withdrawn and must not be reintroduced. A2 is what makes A4 necessary rather than merely economical: once every full suite runs after every cross-verification stage, a late suite failure strands a stale verdict by construction.

options.option: Ratify A4.1 / A4.2 keyed on what changed (test surfaces vs shipped code).
options.consequence: Mechanically decidable from the diff since the recorded round, and defensible: a test-only fix changes nothing that ships, so there is nothing for a verifier to re-examine, while a shipped-code fix gets the cheap tier that already exists (--phase remediation-review reviews only the fix hunks against the recorded discovery baseline). Costs a classifier and its falsifiers, and it is a real reduction: a shipped-code fix now buys a delta review where today it buys an unphased full round.

options.option: Keep the superseded line-count criterion - a fix under two lines owes nothing.
options.consequence: Set 127 S2 planted eight defects against its finished suite to prove its falsifiers bite, and SIX were two lines or fewer - `if (false)`, `const status = row.status`, one inverted ternary - every one a real correctness bug that changed shipped behaviour. A two-line edit is precisely the size that inverts a predicate. Size does not track blast radius, so this waves through exactly the class of change that breaks things.

options.option: No carve-out - any post-suite fix re-opens verification.
options.consequence: The status quo, and the safest possible rule. But under A2 every full suite now runs after every cross-verification stage, so a late suite failure strands a stale verdict by construction: a one-line test fix at the end of a session buys a full metered verification round. That is the wasted cost this set was raised to remove.

operator_attestation: Operator ruling of 2026-08-12, given during Set 127 Session 2 and recorded verbatim in docs/planning/session-step-skeleton-and-verification-cost.md section A4: 'A4.1 - a post-suite fix to one or more tests only (and not to code) does not trigger any re-verification. A4.2 - a post-suite fix to code triggers targeted/focused remediation-review only, not an open re-verification.' The same note flags that this must not be inferred by a later orchestrator and needs its own journalled decision inside the owning set; the operator re-affirmed it at this session's registration stop on 2026-08-12, in the same education-mode brief that carried the depth question journalled beside this record.

question: How deep does the A4 mechanization go? Today ANY post-verification file change - including a one-line test fix - stales the stamped verification row (verification_stamp.validate_stamped_row step 9), so close_session's backstop buys a fresh metered round. A4.1 is therefore contradicted by the machinery, not merely unwritten. Does the classifier only REPORT the obligation, does the close backstop ACT on it, or are test paths excluded from the work-diff digest outright?
decision: The close backstop consults the classifier. A test-only delta since the recorded round lets the existing settling round stand instead of buying a new one; a shipped-code delta runs the delta-scoped remediation-review phase instead of an unphased full round. The work-diff digest, verification_integrity's evidence rules, the round bounds and the no-resurrection rule are all left exactly as they are - the reduction lives in one branch of decide_backstop, is scoped to the one place that spends money, and is ledgered every time it fires. close_backstop.py is therefore touched beyond the spec's declared Touches list; that widening was named to the operator in the brief.

options.option: The close backstop consults the classifier.
options.consequence: Realizes both halves of the ruling at the one place that spends money, and each instance leaves its own auditable record, so a later reader can tell a close that settled under A4.1 from one that verified afterwards. Nothing else moves: the digest still stales on any change, verification_integrity still demands a valid stamped row from a different provider, and the round budget still counts the delta round. About fifty lines in one branch of decide_backstop plus the classifier, and it edits a module the spec did not list under Touches.

options.option: Report only - the classifier plus an advisory report, no gate changes.
options.consequence: Smallest, matches the spec's declared Touches exactly, and weakens nothing at all. But a test-only post-suite fix still stales the row and still buys a full backstop round, so A4.1 remains prose that the machinery contradicts - the exact failure mode this whole set exists to end, and the same shape as the compressed step Session 1 shipped a check against.

options.option: Exclude test paths from the work-diff digest outright.
options.consequence: About five lines instead of fifty, but the risks are structural rather than incidental. It is time-blind: the exclusion applies from the moment of stamping, so a session could verify early and then author or rewrite its entire falsifier suite afterwards with nothing noticing - and in this repo the tests are frequently the deliverable (Session 1 of this set shipped a check plus 12 test functions). It hides test DELETION from the freshness stamp, which collides head-on with Set 118's test retirement, the set Session 3 re-authors. It is a denylist and so fails open on any path left out (L-125-1), and the boundary is genuinely blurry - test-fixtures/ and scripts/ stage what Layer 3 asserts. It leaves no per-instance audit trail. And it mechanizes only A4.1, leaving A4.2's unphased full round in place. The operator was inclined to this option, asked for its risks, and switched on reading them.

operator_attestation: Operator ratified the backstop-consults-the-classifier option at this session's registration stop on 2026-08-12. The education-mode brief named the digest-exclusion option as the operator's own inclination and, at the operator's request, laid out its five risks - time-blindness, invisible test deletion, denylist fail-open, no audit trail, and A4.2 left unmechanized - alongside the sizing of both options; the operator then selected option 1 on that record.

question: Writing A1-A3 into docs/session-constitution.md put it 128 tokens over its 4,000-token preload ceiling, and the corpus has been pinned at 99-100% of every ceiling since Set 085 S2. Raising a preload ceiling is an operator-authorized config edit, never an in-session accommodation. Does this session compress unrelated prose to stay token-neutral, or does the ceiling rise?
decision: The operator issued a STANDING authorization covering all sessions until Set 121 lands, not a one-off for this session. Recorded durably in three places: docs/guidance-lifecycle.md gains a 'Standing operator authorization, 2026-08-12 -> Set 121 (ACTIVE)' section carrying the operator's words verbatim and its three conditions (raise to fit rather than to make room; state the reason in the config comment; Set 121 clears it); ai_router/router-config.yaml carries the matching paragraph beside the ratchet rule it qualifies; and 121-guidance-becomes-executable's Session 4 Step 3 now explicitly owes the retirement - ratchet every ceiling back to the slimmed measurement and delete both notes. This session raised the constitution 4000 -> 4200 and the total 12000 -> 12200, which is raise-to-fit: the file measures 4,084 and the corpus 11,985, so `guidance_report --check` still reports honestly and CI stays green. The three unrelated compressions made before the authorization arrived (the Step 4 checklist parenthetical, the Step 6 no-skip sentence, and the four adjudication options) were REVERTED, so the diff to the constitution is the A1-A4 rules and nothing else.

options.option: Standing authorization until Set 121, with a raise-to-fit rule and a named retirement owner.
options.consequence: Stops every set that touches a preload file from paying a slimming tax that buys nothing - Set 128 S2 spent its first pass compressing three sections it had no other business editing. The gate keeps reporting real percentages and CI stays green, so nothing goes unmeasured. The risk is the classic one: an accommodation nobody retires becomes the norm. Mitigated by naming the retirement as a step in Set 121 Session 4 rather than as a hope, and by writing the expiry into both the canonical doc and the config comment.

options.option: Stay token-neutral - compress unrelated prose to fund the new rules.
options.consequence: What the ratchet rule requires by default, and what this session started doing. But the compressions land in sections the session has no business editing, each one loses a shade of meaning (the four adjudication options, the reason the checklist post must precede the brief), and the reviewer of a test-ordering change has to adjudicate prose edits to the escalation ladder. The corpus is at 100% for structural reasons Set 121 exists to fix, so this tax recurs on every set until then.

options.option: Let the ceiling breach stand and leave the gate failing until Set 121.
options.consequence: Honest about the state, and it needs no config edit. But `guidance_report --check` runs as its own CI job, so every push would be red until Set 121 lands - and a permanently red gate is one people learn to scroll past, which is worse than the bloat it watches for (L-064-12: a red CI is unknown coverage, not passing coverage). Not put to the operator as a serious option.

operator_attestation: Operator, 2026-08-12, in two messages during this session: first 'I authorize you to go over the budget of the guidance. We will be making changes to guidance in a subsequent set.', then, when asked for a durable record, 'Please make a durable note that I hereby authorize all sessions to go over the ceiling on guidance until we fix guidance in set 121.' The second message is quoted verbatim in docs/guidance-lifecycle.md and names both the scope (all sessions) and the expiry (Set 121).

question: Session 1's step-shape check is BLOCKING for unstarted sets, and four are unstarted and non-conforming: 113 (4 sessions), 118 (3), 121 (4) and 122 (3). Session 3 is specced to re-author 118 only. The operator intends to run 122 next, so 122 is blocked today. Where does the restructuring of the other three happen - inside Session 3, or as a new first session added to each set?
decision: Fold all four into Session 3, split by KIND. Step 2 stays substantive: re-author 118 to the new skeleton AND the new ordering, restating its retirement rule in terms of A1/A3 and re-reading its measurements - that is judgment, not text. Step 3 absorbs the MECHANICAL restructuring of 113, 121 and 122 and then re-admits all four through spec_admission. Session 3 stays at N=3 work steps and no new sessions are created anywhere. The dogfood gets stronger rather than diluted: the check is proven on four specs this set did not author. The operator raised the alternative (a new first session in each set) and withdrew it on the evidence below.

options.option: Fold all four into Session 3 - 118 substantively in step 2, the other three mechanically in step 3.
options.consequence: Measured before recommending: all four sets carry the IDENTICAL malformation - a 5-step session whose step 5 compresses verify + full suite + close, most in the wrong internal order. The fix per session is to replace one step with three, giving 7 steps and exactly N=3 work steps, so no sessionSizeException is needed anywhere. Fourteen sessions, one mechanical edit each. Unblocks 122 for the operator to run next, and clears 113 and 121 so nobody trips on the check later. Costs Session 3 a wider step 3.

options.option: Give each unstarted set a new first session that restructures its own spec.
options.consequence: Self-defeating, and this is the decisive point: to ADD a session you must edit the spec, and once you are editing it the restructuring is the same edit and strictly smaller. The added session would also have to satisfy the very check it was created to satisfy. And it spends four ceremony steps (register, verify, full suite, close-out) to perform a text edit - which is precisely the ceremony overhead this set exists to reduce.

options.option: Session 3 does 118 and 122 only; 113 and 121 are restructured by whoever picks them up.
options.consequence: Minimal and timely - it unblocks exactly what the operator plans to run next. But it leaves two sets carrying a known blocking defect, discovered at the least convenient moment (the start of a session, by an orchestrator who did not expect it), for a saving of two mechanical edits.

operator_attestation: Operator, 2026-08-12: 'perhaps we could modify the third session of this set to include restructuring set 122 under the new rules -- alternatively, modify set 122 to include a new first session that does the restructuring. If we take the second approach, it might be better to create new first sessions for sets 113 and 121 (the other not started sets), as well.' Presented with the measured cost of each and the self-defeating property of the second approach, the operator selected folding all four into Session 3.

question: Set 128's spec asserts that restructuring the fourteen unstarted sessions yields 7 steps and exactly N=3 work steps everywhere, so no sessionSizeException is owed - and instructs Session 3 to re-measure rather than trust that sentence. Re-measuring found two sessions whose fifth step was NOT pure ceremony. 113 Session 4 carried 'reserve the follow-on sets' and the set's own dogfood UAT; 121 Session 2 carried 'Argue N and the cap from data; do not inherit them', which has its own progress key (numbersDerived). What happens to genuine work that was compressed into the ceremony step?
decision: Split by whether the compressed content has an independent home. 113 S4: 'reserve the follow-on sets' folded into step 4 (Record the outcome either way), which is already the outcome-recording step, and the dogfood UAT moved into close-out, where disposition.uat is authored and gated anyway - both were already bundled with 'and close' in the original, so this is faithful and 113 S4 lands at 7 steps / N=3. 121 S2: NO fold. Step 5 derives the PARAMETERS (N and the cap) that steps 3 and 4's retention RULES consume, the sequencing note's 4b explicitly flags both as proposed-not-measured, and it carries its own progress key. Merging it would bury a named deliverable in prose - the exact failure mode the skeleton exists to prevent. So 121 S2 declares a sessionSizeException with its reason, at 8 steps / N=4. Thirteen of fourteen sessions needed none; one did, and the spec's sentence is corrected rather than defended.

options.option: Declare a sessionSizeException for 121 Session 2 and fold 113 Session 4's content into existing steps.
options.consequence: Preserves both authors' decompositions and every progress key. The exception is the sanctioned mechanism for a genuine overrun and it states its reason, so it survives review rather than reading as a typo. Costs: the set's own spec claimed no exception was owed anywhere, so that claim is now falsified by measurement - which is what the instruction to re-measure was for.

options.option: Fold 121 Session 2's step 5 into step 3 or step 4 so every session lands at N=3.
options.consequence: Would make the sentence in Set 128's spec true, at the cost of hiding a deliverable the 121 author deliberately separated and the sequencing note deliberately flagged. Optimising the corpus to match a prediction is how a shape check starts producing compliant specs that say less - the same class of harm as the compression this set was built to stop.

options.option: Split 121 into a fifth session so Session 2's work fits at N=3.
options.consequence: Rejected on the same evidence the operator used to withdraw the new-first-session option in Session 2: adding a session spends four ceremony steps and is a larger spec edit than the one it avoids. A one-step overrun does not justify a whole session's overhead.
